title.title: The Correspondence of Esther Roberts Hunt Collins

msIdentifier.institution: Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College

projectDesc.p: The correspondence of Quaker minister Esther Roberts Hunt Collins is stored at the Friends Historical Library of Swarthmore College. With the generous support of H. David and Joyce E. Hunt, Library staff scanned and transcribed these letters in 2024 and encoded the text in TEI.

div.p: Thy letter of the 3rd instant came to hand the 13th, which was long looked for before arrived, that by J. Conn I have not yet received. Affection prompts me to write once more, notwithstanding I have nothing of importance to relate. Our visit to Philadelphia is at an end. For if everything had combined to forward the journey, we are prevented by Mary’s disability, who scalded both her feet with sugar water the first of this month & has walked none since, & appears likely that many weeks will elapse before she will have recovered. She is in good health otherwise, and all the rest of us. Our little boy is fat & hearty & will soon talk. We have not made much sugar yet, & I am calculating to do but little of everything, for I cannot hire to answer. & if I can get clear of George shall do it unless he improves very suddenly.

Mother, I should feel myself happily situated if my family consisted of my wife & son alone, or of persons agreeable, for I hate perplexity. I received a letter from Brother Nathan a few days ago. He did not say one word about his family, but have since understood that thou hast a second grandson.
22nd We have stormy cold disagreeable weather, & the muddiest roads that I ever saw, Mcmanamy’s lane is hub deep to the waggon & we have to ride round by Glade Grist mill every week.

I would be glad to know if horses will sell in Jersey for any reasonable price. Nathan’s mare I have keeping & as I believe she would answer in that country much better than this, I think it will be better to send her, and several others perhaps if there is a probability of their selling. Thou wilt be pleased to inform me by the first mail what demand there likely may be & what such horses as Father’s & thine are worth (I mean those you took from here). Also, what kind are most saleable, for there is not many things that will sell here for cash, & horses may be bought very low for cash.

Nothing to mention relative to our neighborhood. We all move nearly in the usual sphere. Timothy Smith has appealed to the Quarterly Meeting from the judgment of the Monthly. We are to have a trial to make new Elders again, but Mother, we want new judges, or better. I have understood that Edward Brook has a prospect of coming to Meeting at Redstone, which I expect will be an addition & help to our poor & neglected Meeting.

23rd. This day I received a letter from Nathan informing that “on the 15th of last month his wife was brought to bed with a son, on the 18th the child taken with fits and expired in half an hour from the time it appeared bad, his wife had become pretty smart & well except her breast which continued an ugly running sore four holes in it which run much. I also received one from Stacy complaining a little of the want of school. Otherwise he writes cheerfully. I shall endeavor to supply his little wants which are yet quite moderate relative to his schooling. I don’t remember one word about their bargain in any respect, but I think he
He ought to have more schooling, & that Nathan might well afford to give him three months as little enough, for he is surely worth more than his rituals & clothes that he works in. I don’t look at the custom of mechanics so much or what I think is just, however rather than that he should not have it. I’ll board him & pay for his schooling for four times three months whenever he may think it proper to come. Mother, I want thee to tell me if I am indebted to thee for learning more than thy other children. For deficient as I am in literature, I find every Brother to be much more so. Their spelling is generally so bad that I feel sorry they had not a greater opportunity, or would now take more pains. & my dear Sister do though take care of what thou part, & still endeavor to improve by opportunities at home, from thy letters I observe thou dost not spell correctly or art too careless, & dear Sister be thou obedient to thy kind Mother more so than I have been her counsel is for thy good. As I now believe it was formerly to me for mine, I am well assured that her anxiety for me preserved me from much iniquity, if not inevitable ruin. My sister or thou art likely perhaps to fall in company with young men at times. Be thou forever on thy guard. Don’t make thyself too cheap, conduct with modest reserve, which is the beauty of females. Be rather diffident than forward, & don’t laugh too much, it generally indicates a futile and weak mind. Every man of sense admires modestly & soberness in women. & dear Sister, remember that men are exceedingly treacherous. They are filled with deception beyond thy conception. Thou mayest believe me, for the time was that I loved to cheat the girls, and there are many who exalt in it. Therefore watch them.

Mother there has been some talk of our going to town to keep school & it is not very unlikely, but we may receive another invitation, thy sentiments thereon before an engagement might help to convince us of thee right or wrong of such a procedure. Thou mayest write by Ephram Butcher, the bearer of this.

Thy letter by J. Comly has just arrived & I feel thankful that we can converse in this way, although presence & conversation would be still more animating & refreshing. Thou mayest tell Elizabeth Collins that I love her, & every person whom I believe tries to do right continually.
